stops.name: 25 de Abril Bridge
stops.en: This sister bridge of the San Francisco – Oakland Bay Bridge was designed by the same architect in 1966 to connect Lisbon with the Setubal peninsula across the Tagus (Tejo) River. Formerly known as the Salazar Bridge, it was renamed after the Carnation Revolution which, on 25 April 1974, ended the dictatorship.

stops.name: Lisbon Cathedral
stops.en: Built in 1147, the cathedral has survived various earthquakes and has undergone restoration, renovation, and modification over the years. Its elements include Romanesque, Gothic, and Baroque styles. It has been a national monument since 1910.

stops.name: Praça do Comércio
stops.en: This magnificent plaza, facing the river, is the beginning of Lisboa's downtown. It is also known as 'Terreiro do Paço', meaning 'Grounds of the Palace', relating to its function before the Great Earthquake of 1755. The upper floors of the yellow buildings surrounding the square are mainly used as government offices, while the lower floors often contains cafés and restaurants. King Josef I, who ru

stops.name: Castle of Saint George
stops.en: Humans settled on this hill as early as the 8th century BCE, and the first fortifications date from the 1st century BCE. Before the Portuguese conquest in the 1147 Siege of Lisbon, the site was successively occupied by the Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Romans, and Moors. Sights within the castle include the permanent exhibition of archaeological artefacts with an emphasis on the 11th- and 12th-centu

stops.name: Santa Justa Lift
stops.en: Excellent vertical view of the Baixa streets, next to Igreja do Carmo. The line can be quite long, you may want to consider walking up and riding it down instead.

stops.name: National Museum of Ancient Art
stops.en: Portugal's impressive national art collection, including 14-19th century European painting, artefacts of Portuguese contact with the East and Africa and a collection of ecclesiastical treasures. Highlights include Dürer's St Jerome, Hieronymus Bosch's Temptations of St Antony, Nuno Gonçalves' Adoration of St Vincent, and 16th century Japanese paintings of Portuguese traders.

stops.name: Church of Santa Engrácia
stops.en: This is one of the most striking buildings in Lisbon. Its tall dome and white facade makes it a real landmark in Alfama/Eastern Lisbon. Excellent views from the rooftop terrace. Construction began in 1681, then halted until the dome was added in 1966 and then converted to the National Pantheon. Amália Rodrigues, queen of fado, is buried here, and fresh roses can be seen on the tomb. The church als

stops.name: São Bento Palace
stops.en: Built in 1598, the palace has served as the home of Portugal's parliament since 1834. The adjoining São Bento Mansion serves as the prime minister's residence.

stops.name: Águas Livres Aqueduct
stops.en: This is a historic aqueduct in the city of Lisbon, Portugal. It is one of the most remarkable examples of 18th-century Portuguese engineering, including the largest stone arch in the world. The main course of the aqueduct covers 18 km, but the whole network of canals extends through nearly 58 km. The Mãe d'Água (Mother of the Water) reservoir of the Amoreiras, the largest of the water reservoirs,

stops.name: Monastery of São Vicente de Fora
stops.local: Igreja de São Vicente de Fora
stops.en: Started in 1582, this Mannerist monastery wasn't completed until 1629, following the reconstruction of a 1147 church under royal decree. The church houses the Pantheon of the House of Braganza, where many monarchs, consorts, and their offspring are entombed.

stops.name: Estrela Basilica
stops.en: This Neoclassical and Baroque basilica, dedicated to the Sacred Heart of Jesus, was built in the late 1700s by Queen Maria I in fulfilment of a vow. The Queen is entombed in the right transept. Among the artworks is a nativity scene made up of over 500 cork and terracotta figures by Joaquim Machado de Castro.

stops.name: Carmo Convent
stops.en: The hilltop church of the former convent of Carmo is a towering memorial of the 1755 earthquake, which made the roof of the church collapse, but the Gothic arches of the nave survived. The church was preserved that way and now serves as the Museu Arqueológico in the extant parts of the building. The museum houses a hodgepodge of archaeological artifacts from around Portugal and the world including

stops.name: Belém Tower
stops.en: A , the iconic fortified tower was built in the early 16th century in the late Gothic Manueline style as a fortress. It was said to be the last thing Portuguese explorers saw when departing, and the first thing they saw upon return. It was later used as a prison for political prisoners, and is today one of the most recognized symbols of Lisbon and Portugal.

stops.name: Jerónimos Monastery
stops.en: A , the monastery was built in the 16th century and is an outstanding example of the Portuguese late Gothic Manueline style.

stops.name: Vasco da Gama Bridge
stops.en: It is the longest bridge in Europe (including viaducts), and ninth longest in the world, with a total length of , including for the main bridge, in viaducts, and in dedicated access roads.

stops.name: Padrão dos Descobrimentos
stops.en: Climbing the monument gives you a spectacular view of Belém.

stops.name: Calouste Gulbenkian Museum
stops.en: One of the best museums in Lisbon. Created from the personal collection of the art and artifact collector Calouste Gulbenkian. The collection include Egyptian artefacts; Islamic and oriental art; paintings by masters such as Rembrandt, Manet, Monet, Renoir, and Cassat; and a large collection of objects made by the Art Nouveau jeweler René Lalique. Gulbenkian was an Armenian born in the Ottoman Emp

stops.name: Rossio Square
stops.en: One of Lisbon's principal squares. A statue of King Pedro IV stands on a column in the centre. The square, a popular meeting point for local and tourists, is known for its wavy black-and-white stone pavement.

stops.name: Rossio railway station
stops.en: Built in 1890 as the Estação Central (Central Station), it was the main railway hub until 1957. It provides a direct connection to Sintra in about 40 min. The trains access the station through a 2.6-km long tunnel. The main facade is an example of the Neo-Manueline style, a revival of Gothic style in Portugal during the mid-19th century.

stops.name: National Azulejo Museum
stops.en: One of the most important national museums, dedicated to Portuguese azulejo tiles since the late 1400s. It's in the former Madre de Deus Convent, founded in 1509 by Queen Leonor.

stops.name: Lisbon Oceanarium
stops.en: One of the world's largest aquariums. Built by American architect Peter Chermayeff, it hosts thousands of marine species of the oceans, such as sea otters, penguins, and sharks. The main tank is huge, representing the Atlantic environment, with hundreds of small fishes, sharks, barracuda, snappers, and a huge sunfish. Ideal for children.

stops.name: Belém Cultural Center
stops.en: CCB is a complex of artistic and cultural venues. It has spaces for meetings and conferences, performing arts (film, opera, ballet, theatre, and music), and art exhibits (art, architecture, design, and photography).

stops.name: Tejo Power Station
stops.en: This disused power station is now a museum dedicated to the science, industry, and history of electricity production in Portugal.

stops.name: Lisbon Zoo
stops.en: A zoo that is fairly pricey, but has a variety of exotic animals featuring sea-lions and dolphins.

stops.name: National Coach Museum
stops.en: Housed in the former riding school of the palace, don't miss the world's largest collection of horse-drawn coaches and other royal vehicles. One of Lisbon's many unusual museums. In the "Museum street", Belem.

stops.name: Prazeres Cemetery
stops.en: This large cemetery is packed with majestic gravestones and mausoleums, separated by wide, pedestrian, tree-lined "streets". Many graves are marked with icons telling something about the person's role in historical Lisbon. A beautiful respite from the busy city.

stops.name: Jardim Botânico de Lisboa
stops.en: A hidden gem. It was created several hundred years ago, by a King of Portugal at the time of the Discoveries. The story goes that this King wanted one of every type of plant in the world, and although that's unlikely, there is a huge collection dating back by three or four centuries which is worth checking out. And there's something quite eerie about seeing plants or huge trees from completely dif

stops.name: Church of Nossa Senhora da Conceição Velha
stops.en: 18th-century Manueline-style church, a national monument.

stops.name: Jardim da Estrela
stops.en: A English-style garden with Romantic inspiration. You can find many plant and bird species here.

stops.name: Ancient Roman theatre
stops.local: Ruínas do teatro romano de Lisboa
stops.en: Along the way from downtown to Saint George's Castle.

stops.name: Design Museum
stops.en: The collection has about 1,000 items of furniture and accessories and over 1,200 pieces of haute couture clothing.

stops.name: Museu Militar de Lisboa
stops.en: Housed in a 16th-century foundry, this museum holds its testaments to Portuguese military history, and contains many artifacts, including a sword used by Vasco da Gama.

stops.name: Palácio Alverca
stops.en: Unassuming from the outside, the interior combines neo-Gothic, neo-Arab, neo-Renaissance, neo-Rococo, Art Nouveau, and baroque elements.

stops.name: Pavilhão do Conhecimento - Ciência Viva Science Centre
stops.en: Ciência Viva is an interactive science and technology museum that aims to make science accessible to all, stimulating experimentation and exploration of the physical world.

stops.name: European Union Drugs Agency
stops.local: Observatório Europeu da Droga e da Toxicodependência

stops.name: Freguesia de São Vicente de Fora
Freguesia de São Sebastião da Pedreira
Praça da Figueira
stops.en: This large square has an equestrian statue of King João I. An important transport hub, the square is surrounded by hotels, cafés, and shops in four-storey buildings dating back to the rebuilding after the 1755 Great Earthquake.

stops.name: Restauradores Square
stops.en: This major square lies at the southeast end of Avenida da Liberdade. The Monument to the Restorers, a obelisk commemorating the 1640 restoration of Portugal as a kingdom separate from Spain, sits in the middle of the square.

stops.name: Navy Museum
stops.en: One of the most important in Europe, evoking Portugal's domination of the seas. Its colossal 17,000 items are installed in the west wing of Jerónimos Monastery, and include model ships from the Age of Discovery onward. The oldest exhibit is a wooden figure representing the Archangel Raphael that accompanied Vasco da Gama on his voyage to India.

stops.name: Edward VII Park
stops.en: Formal park with expansive views down toward the city and water from Miradouro Parque Eduardo VII. Home to the wonderful Estufa Fria greenhouse gardens.

stops.name: Marquess of Pombal Square
stops.en: Essentially a large roundabout with a sizeable statue of a former Portuguese prime minister in the middle.

stops.name: Museum of Art, Architecture and Technology
stops.local: Museu de Arte, Arquitetura e Tecnologia
stops.en: This museum of contemporary art is housed in a riverside building of contemporary design.

stops.name: Berardo Collection Museum
stops.local: Museu de Arte Contemporânea do Centro Cultural de Belém
stops.en: The permanent collection of the museum consists of the Berardo Collection, which is made up of modern and contemporary art, with major art movements like abstract expressionism, Abstraction-Création, action painting, body Art, constructivism, cubism, De Stijl, digital art, experimental art, geometric abstraction, kinetic art, minimal art, neo-expressionism, neo-plasticism, neo-Realism, op art, pho

stops.name: Miradouro de Santa Luzia
stops.en: Good viewpoint in Alfama uphill from the cathedral along tram route. Lovely view over rooftops and river.

stops.name: Jardim de São Pedro de Alcântara
stops.en: Excellent panorama from the lovely terrace/garden on top of Elevador da Glória and northern corner of Bairro Alto.

stops.name: Centro de Arte Moderna Gulbenkian
stops.en: A museum dedicated to art since the 1950s, focusing on Portuguese artists and including other nationalities, notably British and Armenian. Part of the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation.

stops.name: Miradouro da Senhora do Monte
stops.en: The highest viewpoint in Lisbon, at the top of the Graça hill, spread out in front of the small Capela de Nossa Senhora do Monte (founded in 1147, remodelled in the 20th century). To the south you look down over the Castelo de São Jorge, the Mouraria and the Baixa to the Tagus estuary; to the west, from Bairro Alto out to the Monsanto forest; to the north, down the Avenida Almirante Reis valley. I

stops.name: Museu da Marioneta
stops.en: The museum covers the history of puppetry around the world, with an emphasis on Portugal. Various types of puppets are on display.

stops.name: Feira Internacional de Lisboa
stops.en: This venue, the size of 11 football pitches, hosts trade shows and similar exhibitions.

stops.name: Planetário de Marinha
stops.en: The planetarium has 32 star projectors, capable of presenting more than 9,000 stars. It holds a chunk of moon rock given by U.S. President Richard Nixon.

stops.name: Museu Arpad Szenes - Vieira da Silva
stops.en: This museum is installed in the restored 18th-century former Royal Silk Factory. Its permanent collection covers a wide time period of the works of 20th-century painters Arpad Szenes and Maria Helena Vieira da Silva, and regularly hosts exhibits by their contemporaries.

stops.name: Jardim Garcia d'Orta
stops.en: A pleasant riverside garden with sculptures and other artworks.

stops.name: Museu da Sociedade de Geografia
stops.en: Exhibits of ethnography from Portugal's former colonies.

stops.name: Ajuda Botanical Gardens
stops.en: The botanical garden of Ajuda is one of the oldest gardens in Europe and is considered the first in Portugal. After the earthquake that occurred in 1755, the homeless Portuguese royal family decided to build a new royal residence at Ajuda but also gardens around it. This 10-acre garden was laid out in from 1858-1873.

stops.name: Palácio Foz
stops.en: A palace constructed in the 18th and 19th centuries. Visits can be arranged in advance via email. Concerts (some of them free) are offered.

stops.name: Espaço Novo Banco
stops.en: Multifunctional space dedicated to contemporary art, especially photography.

stops.name: Statue to Afonso de Albuquerque
stops.en: In front of the former Royal Palace of Belém, now the Presidential Palace, there is a massive statue looking out to sea, representing Afonso de Albuquerque, second ruler of Portuguese India in the early 16th century.

stops.name: Museu da Carris
stops.en: Transport museum with various old trams and buses on display.

eats.name: Leitaria Camponeza
eats.note: On the location of a historical café (the leitaria), this place focuses on only a short number of dishes (meats, fish and seafood) but makes up for this in quality and portion size. For an atmospheric

eats.name: Mercado da Praça da Figueira
eats.note: From the pavement looks like a small convenience shop, on walking in you realize the deception when confronted by the large cavernous meandering interior space, replete with everything expected from a

eats.name: Mercado Oriental
eats.note: A food court serving Asian street food and the only place in Lisbon where you can try Macanese cuisine (at a stall called "Taberna Macau").

eats.name: Néctar WineBar
eats.note: A place dedicated to the promotion of Portugal's wine and gastronomic culture, and featuring a daily lunch menu of Portuguese and Mediterranean cuisine. The wine list comprises – in its vast majority

eats.name: Restaurante Bonjardim
eats.note: Appropriately nicknamed Rei dos Frangos, this is home to the best greasy spit-roasted chicken this side of Louisiana.

eats.name: Restaurante Gambrinus
eats.note: A restaurant-bar which is one of the most chic places in the city. Highly recognized in Lisbon as something of an institution, it attracts an eclectic crowd where the appeal is food and a great select

eats.name: Bar Trobadores
eats.note: Medieval bar in downtown with a cozy atmosphere and a diverse range of traditional Portuguese delicacies. National and international beers.

eats.name: Café Martinho da Arcada
eats.note: Established in 1782, this is the oldest continuously-operating café in Lisbon and throughout its history has been associated with important politicians, writers, and intellectuals. Writer Fernando Pes

eats.name: Restaurante Tascardoso
eats.note: Standing-room only, this place serves simple and affordable Portuguese dishes, including grilled sardines. Toilets available.

eats.name: Taberna Minhota
eats.note: A tapas restaurant

eats.name: Time Out Market
eats.note: The late 19th-century market was closed in 2000, and in 2014 the publisher Time Out Portugal transformed the space into a gourmet food court with 40 kiosks, including restaurants, bars, and shops. A n

eats.name: Rosa da Rua Restaurante
eats.note: A traditional restaurant offering an interesting mix of Portuguese, Indian, and Cape Verdean flavours. The lunch-time buffet offers excellent value for money and great quality food. Staff are patient

eats.name: Faca & Garfo
eats.note: A cozy and affordable restaurant which offers tasty grilled Portuguese specialities of meat and fish.

eats.name: Bengal Tandoori
eats.note: Cuisine of East Bengal, India, using a tandoor oven.

eats.name: Cervejaria da Trindade
eats.note: This excellent restaurant-brewery in a former monastery has several kinds of Sagres beer and Guinness. The appetizer that is charged for each item that is consumed separately. Nice codfish plates.

eats.name: Os Tibetanos
eats.note: Vegetarian restaurant affiliated with a Buddhist center. Vegan friendly. Juice bar.

eats.name: Tamarind
eats.note: Small Indian restaurant. Reservations can be made online.

eats.name: Restaurante Brasuca
eats.note: Great Brazilian food served by friendly staff.

eats.name: Restaurante Calcutá 2
eats.note: The second of two restaurants operated by the same owners. Decent Indian food, but far from the best. The location is great though for starting a night out on the town. Ask for the shoot drinks!

eats.name: Restaurante Lisboa À Noite
eats.note: A restaurant with a variety of traditional Portuguese dishes very appreciated by the tourists. Friendly environment, great service. Make sure you try the appetizers.

eats.name: Restaurante Sacramento do Chiado
eats.note: A popular locals' place in palace stables from the 18th-century . The atmosphere and the food are excellent. Service is very good and the recommendations by the staff are outstanding. The writing on t

eats.name: Restaurante Sinal Vermelho
eats.note: Good traditional Portuguese at reasonable prices.

eats.name: Restaurante Terra
eats.note: Probably the best vegetarian restaurant in Lisbon and also the nicest in terms of ambience and service. They have a menu in English and will help with vegan choices or people with other dietary restri

eats.name: Come Prima
eats.note: Traditional Italian fresh pasta dishes, various starters, risottos, meats and wood-oven pizzas are produced from a wide selection of prime quality fresh ingredients. Extensive wine list procured from

eats.name: Café Buenos Aires
eats.note: A good and selected combination of cheap and mid range dishes. The owners are very friendly and speak English, as well as Portuguese. It is a good restaurant if you want to eat South American grilled

eats.name: Belcanto
eats.note: Contemporary Portuguese cuisine with two Michelin stars.

eats.name: Alma
eats.note: Two-Michelin-star fine dining by chef Henrique Sá Pessoa, blending traditional Portuguese cuisine with Asian influences. Choose from two tasting menus or order à la carte.

eats.name: Loco Restaurante
eats.note: Michelin-starred restaurant offering two tasting menus using local ingredients by chef Alexandre Silva, who won the first series of Top Chef de Portugal.

eats.name: 100 Maneiras
eats.note: Michelin-starred restaurant by Bosnian chef Ljubomir Stanisic, who blends influences from his homeland, his adopted country, and elsewhere around the globe.

eats.name: Epur
eats.note: Michelin-starred restaurant by French chef Vincent Farges, who prepares an edgy surprise menu centred on visual elegance and purity of flavours.

eats.name: Café A Brasileira
eats.note: One of Lisbon's remaining classic cafés, with a restaurant in the basement; despite renovation, not much has changed since the 1920s. The café was Fernando Pessoa's favourite place, and a statue of th

eats.name: Manteigaria - Fábrica de Pastéis de Nata
eats.note: A bakery serving some of the best pastéis de nata in town, arguably the best in Lisbon. You can even watch them make the pasteis de nata. Standing room only.

eats.name: Chafariz do Vinho
eats.note: Perfect place to linger over a glass of wine at this wine bar that is under the arches of the city's former acquaducts. With a great selection of appetizers that are matched perfectly with the wine, i

eats.name: Garrafeira Alfaia
eats.note: Nice wine bar with an impressive selection of good wines and appetizers. Good place to spend the late afternoon, before going out to dinner.

eats.name: Tivoli Hotel Sky Bar
eats.note: The superbly located rooftop bar of Tivoli Hotel is a small secret. On warm evenings one of the best places to have an overpriced late drink. Youngish music late night.

eats.name: Fado In Chiado
eats.note: Fado In Chiado - Daily show (except on Sundays) at 19:00, with a duration of 50 minutes. Voices that sing the Fado to the sound of Portuguese guitar.

eats.name: Tasca do Chico
eats.note: A cramped but authentic Fado bar.

eats.name: Restaurante Santa Rita
eats.note: Authentic, cheap Portuguese dishes in a very busy, shared-table restaurant.

eats.name: Velha Gaiteira
eats.note: A charming spot with a welcoming host. A delicious prix fixe meal was €12.50.

eats.name: Chapitô à Mesa
eats.note: Great views are the main feature if you reserve terrace seat in advance. Good atmosphere; international-menu food is tasty but nothing special.

eats.name: Farol de Santa Luzia
eats.note: Great place to have typical Portuguese food before climbing to Castelo S. Jorge.

eats.name: Malmequer Bemmequer
eats.note: Friendly and inexpensive; long menu of traditional Portuguese dishes.

eats.name: Portuel Kosher Store
eats.note: Lisbon's source for kosher groceries.

eats.name: Zambeze
eats.note: A Mozambique restaurant on a "miradouro", viewing spot, offering a great view of the river, the Baixa area, and beyond. An elevator can bring you up and down the deep slopes, making it easily reachabl

eats.name: Lux Fragil
eats.note: It's in a former warehouse and part owned by American actor John Malkovich.

eats.name: Pois Café
eats.note: It's a place to relax, read a book, drink a coffee and plan your way around Lisbon. Also offers toasts, pastas, quiches and salads; features late breakfasts.

eats.name: Portas do Sol
eats.note: A cafe and bar on a "Miradouro", viewing spot, and thus offer a spectacular view over the Alfama rooftops down to the river.

eats.name: Eneko Lisboa
eats.note: Michelin-starred restaurant by Spanish Basque chef Eneko Atxa. Attached to a more laid-back space called "Basque".

eats.name: Feitoria
eats.note: Michelin-starred seafood restaurant by the docks.

eats.name: A Marítima do Restelo
eats.note: Seafood restaurant by the water.

eats.name: Prova - Enoteca
eats.note: Modern, urban wine bar serving seafood and sausage & cheese platters in a convivial atmosphere.

eats.name: Taberna dos Ferreiros
eats.note: A fresh take on Mediterranean cuisine.

eats.name: Pastéis de Belém
eats.note: The most famous of pastelarias, and justly so. They are served right out of the oven there, with the side of confectioner's sugar and cinnamon. As you navigate through the tile-covered labyrinthine pa

eats.name: A Avó Tinha
eats.note: A modern take on traditional Portuguese dishes.

eats.name: D'Bacalhau
eats.note: Specializing in cod, they also serve steaks and other fish. It's along the river with nice views from the upstairs dining room.

eats.name: Fifty Seconds
eats.note: Michelin-starred restaurant by Spanish chef Martín Berasategui, in the Myriad Sana Hotel up the Vasco da Gama Tower, offering spectacular views.

eats.name: Oásis Vegetariano
eats.note: Vegetarian and vegan dishes.

eats.name: Páteo Restaurante
eats.note: Traditional Portuguese cuisine.

eats.name: O Cubo
eats.note: A place for a family meal or a business lunch.

eats.name: Eleven
eats.note: Michelin-starred restaurant in Jardim Amália Rodrigues with views of Parque Eduardo VII.

eats.name: Fábrica Imperial
eats.note: They say they serve grandma's cooking with the love of a grandchild.

eats.name: Il Gattopardo
eats.note: An elegant restaurant serving fashionable gourmet Italian.

next.name: Fátima
next.note: Fátima — the city and the Marian shrine of the worldwide famous apparitions of the Virgin Mary

next.name: Nazaré
next.note: Nazaré — a lovely village that became an international surf spot and entered the Guinness Book of Records for its gigantic sea waves

next.name: Tomar
next.note: Tomar — the city of the Knights Templar: it is highly recommended to visit the medieval castle and the Convent of Christ

next.name: Óbidos
next.note: Óbidos — a beautiful village dominated by an old medieval castle

next.name: Mafra
next.note: Mafra — A charming town with a monastery.

next.name: Ericeira
next.note: Ericeira — A gorgeous seaside resort near Mafra, well known to surfers worldwide.

next.name: Sintra
next.note: Sintra — A beautiful UNESCO World Heritage site town 40 minutes by car/train from Lisbon.

next.name: Sintra
next.note: Praia das Maçãs — A small and surprisingly calm seaside resort about to the west of Lisbon, near the towns of Colares & Sintra.

next.name: Cascais
next.note: Cascais — A pretty town on the bay of the same name, on the Estoril coast, 40 minutes by train from Lisbon (Cais do Sodre Station).

next.name: Almada
next.note: Almada — A city connected to/from Lisbon via ferry boats at Cacilhas and connected by train at Pragal and roadway via 25 Abril bridge/ponte 25 de Abril. The monument of Christ-King (Cristo-Rei) is in Pragal, Almada.

next.name: Setúbal
next.note: Setúbal — Capital of the district, and starting point for visits to Arrábida Nature Park, Troia, and the Sado river. Dolphins can be spotted on the bay.
